requirement:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297

#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.summary: The source generator templates for the object formatter, string-key formatter, enum formatter and union formatter now emit `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on each generated formatter class. The resolver and composite-resolver templates emit it on the resolver class and on their nested `FormatterCache<T>` / `...GetFormatterHelper` classes. Every attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK ... #endif`. One line in `TransformUtilities` now ends the `{` of a constrained nesting type with a line break, so the `#if` directive starts on its own line. The change also regenerates 222 snapshot files, adds a README note and adds a new test class with two tests.
story.why: REQ-2297 asks that all MessagePack generated code carry `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`, so generated code does not skew coverage numbers.
touches_beyond_requirement: TransformUtilities.cs line 58 changes generator output whitespace for generic nesting types with constraints. This is needed so the new `#if` directive starts at the beginning of a line.
README.md gains two sentences. One of them asserts that the attribute is unavailable on netstandard2.0/.NET Framework, which looks factually wrong.
The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard is a design decision the requirement did not ask for. It means consumers on those targets get no exclusion at all.
story.confidence_overview: High that each template now emits the guarded attribute, since the .tt and .cs edits match and the snapshots change uniformly (S1, S2). Medium that this fully meets 'all generated code'. The guard drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework, which do appear to have this attribute, so those users get nothing. The second new test is weaker than its comment says: it only asserts that at least one guarded occurrence exists per file. Composite resolver output and the TransformUtilities newline fix are not exercised by the new tests; only by snapshot tests whose method names are not in the diff.

claims.text: When a nesting type has generic constraints, the opening brace is now followed by CRLF. This ensures the `#if` directive emitted next starts at the beginning of a line; a directive mid-line would not compile.

breaker.reason: Checked TransformUtilities.cs line 58 against all 6 templates—specifically StringKeyFormatterTemplate.cs line 37 and UnionTemplate.cs line 30, which emit '#if' immediately after EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces without a leading newline—and confirmed via static check S2 (HasPrivateSerializedMemberAndIsGenericNamedFormatter) that without CRLF after '{' when anyConstraints is true, '#if' would land right after '{' on the same line and fail C# compilation.

refusals.what: The ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute is added to the user-declared partial resolver class, changing metadata on a possibly public user type and risking duplicate-attribute build errors.
refusals.why: Generated output merged into users' own (possibly public) types is user-visible. A design choice that can break existing builds should be decided by the owner.

refusals.what: The test claims to verify that every attribute occurrence is guarded but only asserts at least one is.
refusals.why: The test checks less than its comment says.

refusals.what: The README asserts the attribute is unavailable on netstandard2.0/.NET Framework, justifying a guard that drops the feature there.
refusals.why: The documentation appears factually wrong and narrows the requirement ('all generated code') without saying so.

Furthermore, REQ-2297 is only partly met due to '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' at ResolverTemplate.tt line 14 and ResolverTemplate.cs line 38.

Claim C6 disputed: REQ-2297 ('all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute') is only partly met because ResolverTemplate.tt lines 31 and 48 and ResolverTemplate.cs lines 55 and 67 guard ExcludeFromCodeCoverage with '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK', omitting the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets even though ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is available in both.

Claim C7 disputed: REQ-2297 ('all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute') is only partly met because CompositeResolverTemplate.tt lines 7 and 35 and CompositeResolverTemplate.cs lines 27 and 56 guard ExcludeFromCodeCoverage with '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK', omitting the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets where ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists.

Claim C10 disputed: C10 misdescribes the cited TestSource (CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs lines 21-62): it omits the second [MessagePackObject] int-key class MyUnionMember (lines 48-53) and misses that MyEnum (lines 37-41) is unreferenced by any serializable member, so generated.Count >= 5 (line 71) passes via those 5 attributed types without generating an enum formatter. Also, REQ-2297 is only partly met and tested because CompositeResolver is unexercised and netstandard2.0 / .NET Framework targets are excluded.

Claim C13 disputed: REQ-2297 ('MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute') is only partly met in the regenerated snapshots because every added attribute is wrapped in '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' (for example MessagePack.GeneratedMessagePackResolver.g.cs lines 12, 29, and 46), leaving netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework builds undecorated. Also, two formatter snapshots in GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember—not one—had brace-newline reshaping (+5/-1 on HasPrivateSerializedMemberAndIsGenericNamedFormatter.g.cs and +4/-0 on HasPrivateSerializedMemberAndIsGenericOrdinalFormatter.g.cs).

The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` omits the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` appears to exist on .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, with class targets supported. Consumers on those targets therefore get no exclusion, contrary to 'all generated code'. The same guard is used in every template.

The attribute is applied to the user's `partial class` resolver, so it merges with the user's own declaration. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their resolver partial would hit CS0579 (duplicate attribute) and the build would break. The attribute would also silently exclude any user-written code in that partial class. The same applies to CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8.
The comment says every attribute occurrence must be guarded, but the test only asserts `guardedCount > 0`. An unguarded attribute alongside one guarded attribute in the same file would pass.
The output compilation and diagnostics are discarded (`out _, out _`), so the new tests do not verify that the generated code with the `#if` directives compiles.
The README states the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework. This appears inaccurate and would mislead users.

Emitting [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on the generated 'partial class <ResolverName>' declaration (and likewise in CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8 / CompositeResolverTemplate.cs line 27) decorates a user-declared partial class. Because ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has AllowMultiple = false, any consumer who already placed [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their own partial resolver class as a workaround for issue #2297 will hit compile error CS0579 (Duplicate 'ExcludeFromCodeCoverage' attribute). In addition, class-level [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] applies across all partial declarations, silently excluding any handwritten user methods in that partial class from code coverage.

All 6 code templates (FormatterTemplate.tt:14, StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt:18, EnumTemplate.tt:8, UnionTemplate.tt:10, ResolverTemplate.tt:14/31/48, CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7/35) wrap [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] in '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK'. Parameterless System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has been in the BCL since .NET Framework 4.0 and .NET Standard 2.0 (only the Justification property requires .NET 5+), so netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers unnecessarily get no [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on generated code.

In TestSource, 'public enum MyEnum' is never referenced by any [MessagePackObject] member, so MessagePackGenerator never emits an enum formatter in CodeCoverageExclusionTests. Because MyUnionMember (lines 48-53) also has [MessagePackObject], generated.Count is 5 without MyEnum, causing Assert.True(generated.Count >= 5) at line 71 to pass while leaving EnumTemplate completely untested by CodeCoverageExclusionTests.
